description: We have all felt dizzy upon standing up too quickly and wondered, "Am I really that old?" Now, imagine an astronaut who, after months in microgravity, lands and gravity pulls their blood back down into their legs, potentially causing them to faint. On the Moon or Mars, there would be no rescue. We are developing an app that provides step-by-step guidance through a standing test to determine whether the astronaut is ready to walk, should wait, or ought to remain where they are.
summary:
I developed a health-monitoring and decision-support application to address orthostatic hypotension during landing and gravitational alteration throughout a mission. 

It guides the crew member through a simple, staged standing-tolerance check, collects heart-rate and blood-pressure readings alongside reported symptoms, and presents a clear next-step recommendation. Its purpose is to verify the astronaut’s current response to standing in front of orthostatic hipotension risks.

After a transition to a different gravity environment, an astronaut may have difficulty maintaining blood pressure while standing. This orthostatic intolerance can cause dizziness or fainting. On the Moon or Mars, immediate medical assistance or a recovery team may not be available, making the first minutes after landing a critical moment for autonomous health decisions.
details:
What exactly does it do?

MerluHealth is a decision-support app for the first minutes after a crew lands on the Moon or Mars, when no recovery team is waiting. After months in microgravity, standing up can cause dizziness or fainting (orthostatic intolerance). MerluHealth estimates that risk as low, moderate, high or undetermined, with the factors behind it shown on screen. It then guides a short standing test (lying 5 min, sitting 30 s, standing 3 min) and ends with a clear decision card: “Can walk”, “Wait and lie down”, “Do not go out yet”, or “Insufficient data”. It also includes a pre-entry preparation checklist (fluid loading, compression garment, cooling) and a mission log that queues entries to be sent to Earth.

How does it work?

The app follows events: It stays passive during descent and only starts once the crew confirms they're safe and a rest period is done. A transparent rule engine combines heart rate, blood pressure, fluid intake, countermeasure compliance, mission duration and symptoms. A missing or outdated value is never treated as normal. During the test it compares blood pressure and heart rate between lying and standing, using the published clinical criterion for orthostatic hypotension (a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 diastolic). Any severe symptom stops the test and overrides everything else. Data comes from a simulator with three fictional astronauts, manual entry, or an optional Bluetooth heart-rate sensor. Everything runs locally in a single file, so it works offline. Every threshold is editable and labeled by origin: clinical criterion, reference, or provisional.

What benefits does it have? A safer first step: it replaces guesswork with a structured check at the moment when help is minutes or hours away.

It's honest: it estimates and verifies, it does not predict. It shows its reasons, says when it lacks data, and labels simulated data and provisional thresholds.

Usable under stress: large text, high contrast, optional voice guidance, and a symptom-stop button always on screen.

Usable without earth: it runs offline, and with a communication delay of up to ~20 minutes at Mars, the crew does not wait for a reply to protect themselves.

Auditable: each decision is logged with the data and rules that produced it, ready to sync later.

What is the intended impact?

I want to fill a real gap in lunar and Mars surface operations. MerluHealth aims to make the first steps after a Moon or Mars landing safer. After months in microgravity, standing up can cause dizziness or fainting, and NASA expects no rescue crews or medical care after those landings. Our app gives the crew a structured way to check whether they can stand and walk, and a clear decision: can walk, wait and lie down, or do not go out yet. The impact we want is fewer falls and injuries in the most unsupervised minutes of a mission, and a decision aid that crews can trust because it shows its reasons and says when it lacks data. It is a prototype and a decision aid, not a medical device. I see its value as a starting point for validation with space medicine experts

What tools did you use to develop the project?

Languages and code: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, in a single self-contained file with no frameworks or third-party libraries. It runs offline in any modern browser and stores data locally.

Browser features (optional): Web Bluetooth, for a heart-rate sensor, and the Web Speech API, for voice guidance.

Fonts: Barlow Condensed, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono, from Google fonts (open license)

SI: Claude (Anthropic), for UX design and writing part of the code. I directed the concept and reviewed the results

Testing: Node.js and Playwright (headless Chrome), with unit tests for the rule engine and an end-to-end test of the guided flow.

Presentation: LibreOffice Impress, exported to PDF and shared through Google Drive.

Hardware: none required. The demo uses a simulated astronaut. A Bluetooth heart-rate sensor and a blood pressure cuff are supported as optional inputs, but we have not tested them with a real device.

How is your project creative?

I aim at a different problem, most tools monitor vital signs continuously. We act in one critical window, the first minutes after landing, and it ends in a decision.

What factors did your team consider?

Scientific limits: an in-flight leg-cuff test did not predict which astronauts developed hypotension, and heart rate alone was not enough. So the app does not claim to predict, and it uses published clinical criteria only as demo parameters.

Safety: any severe symptom stops the test and overrides everything else. A clean test does not give the green light if the prior estimate is high. A “can walk” result expires and must be repeated.

Data quality: each reading has a source, a time and a plausible range. Missing, stale or out-of-range values are flagged instead of assumed normal.

Autonomy: with up to ~20 minutes of delay each way at Mars, the crew cannot wait for Earth. The app works offline and logs decisions to sync later.

Ethics: sex, mission duration and destination gravity are shown as context and never decide the level by themselves. Demo data is synthetic, and the app is not presented as a medical device.
